title: Graph Theory Basics
tagline: Vertices, edges, and the elegant theorems connecting them: graph theory is the mathematical backbone of networks, routing, scheduling, and social systems.

sections.content:
Open Google Maps and ask for directions — underneath the familiar blue line is a graph of intersections connected by road segments, and the routing engine is running a shortest-path algorithm on it. Log in to Facebook and the system checks a graph of users connected by friendships to suggest who you might know. Install a Python package and pip resolves a directed graph of dependencies to decide what to download first. A compiler assigns registers by colouring a graph of variable lifetimes. Networks, schedules, circuits, social systems, molecular bonds — **graphs are everywhere**, and graph theory is the mathematical language that lets us reason about all of them with the same set of tools.

A **graph** G = (V, E) is deceptively simple: a set of **vertices** (also called nodes) V and a set of **edges** E that connect pairs of vertices. That is all. Yet from this sparse definition emerges one of the richest branches of mathematics and computer science, with deep theorems and practical algorithms that every software engineer encounters sooner or later.

Graphs come in many flavours. An **undirected** graph treats each edge as symmetric — if A is connected to B then B is connected to A, like a mutual friendship. A **directed** graph (or **digraph**) gives each edge an arrow, like a one-way street or a task that must happen before another. Edges can carry **weights** — costs, distances, capacities — making the graph weighted. Special cases like **trees**, **DAGs** (directed acyclic graphs), and **bipartite graphs** arise so often that they have their own rich theory.

In this chapter we build graph theory from the ground up: precise definitions, the fundamental theorems (handshaking lemma, Euler's theorem, tree characterisations), representations in code, traversal algorithms, colouring, and the famous boundary between polynomial and NP-complete problems that Eulerian and Hamiltonian paths straddle. By the end you will be able to model novel problems as graphs and choose the right algorithm to solve them.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Graph G = (V, E)"] --> B["Undirected\nedges are symmetric"]
    A --> C["Directed (Digraph)\nedges are arrows"]
    B --> D["Weighted\nedges have numeric cost"]
    B --> E["Unweighted\nedges are just connections"]
    C --> F["DAG\nDirected Acyclic Graph"]
    C --> G["General Digraph\nmay have cycles"]
    B --> H["Tree\nconnected + acyclic"]
    H --> I["|E| = |V| - 1"]
sections.caption: Graph taxonomy: every special graph type is a restriction of the general (V, E) definition. Trees are the most constrained useful structure.

sections.title: Cities, Roads, and the Degree of a Hub
sections.content:
Picture a map of cities connected by roads. Each city is a **vertex**. Each road is an **edge**. The **degree** of a city is the number of roads directly attached to it — London with 8 motorways radiating out has degree 8. A tiny village with one road connecting it to the nearest town has degree 1 (we call it a **leaf**).

Now imagine hosting a party. Every time two guests shake hands, that is one edge between two vertices. The **handshaking lemma** observes something almost obvious once you see it: every handshake is counted by exactly two people — the two who shook hands. So the total number of times people counted their handshakes (the sum of all degrees) must equal twice the number of handshakes (twice the number of edges). This gives the formula Σ deg(v) = 2|E|, and it implies that the number of people who shook hands an odd number of times is always even — you can never have exactly 1, 3, or 5 odd-degree guests at any party.

A **path** through the city map visits cities in sequence without repeating any city. A **cycle** is a path that returns to where it started. A **tree** is the minimally connected map: there is exactly one path between any two cities. Remove one road and the map disconnects into two parts. Add one road between any two cities and you create exactly one cycle. Trees are simultaneously the most economical and the most fragile connected structures — a single broken edge partitions them.

sections.title: Core Definitions — Vertices, Edges, and Degree
sections.content:
Let us be precise about vocabulary, because graph theory proofs depend on exact definitions.

A **simple graph** has no **self-loops** (an edge from a vertex to itself) and no **parallel edges** (multiple edges between the same pair of vertices). Most graphs we discuss in algorithms are simple. A **multigraph** allows parallel edges; a **pseudograph** also allows self-loops.

The **degree** of a vertex v in an undirected graph, written deg(v), is the number of edges incident to v. A self-loop, if allowed, contributes 2 to the degree. In a **directed graph**, each vertex has an **in-degree** (edges pointing into it) and an **out-degree** (edges pointing out). A **source** vertex has in-degree 0; a **sink** has out-degree 0.

The **handshaking lemma** for undirected graphs states: Σ_{v ∈ V} deg(v) = 2|E|. The proof is one line: each edge contributes exactly 1 to each of its two endpoints' degrees, so each edge contributes exactly 2 to the total sum. The corollary — that every graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices — follows because the sum (an even number) minus the contribution of even-degree vertices (also even) leaves an even residue, which can only be expressed as a sum of an even count of odd numbers.

For directed graphs: Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E|. Each directed edge contributes exactly 1 to some vertex's in-degree and exactly 1 to some vertex's out-degree.

A **walk** from u to v is a sequence of vertices and edges where consecutive vertices share an edge; vertices and edges may repeat. A **trail** is a walk where no edge is repeated. A **path** is a walk where no vertex (hence no edge) is repeated. A **closed walk** returns to the start; a **cycle** is a closed path (start = end, no other repetition).

A graph is **connected** if there exists a path between every pair of vertices. A **connected component** is a maximal connected subgraph — the largest subset of vertices that are mutually reachable. A graph with one component is connected; disconnected graphs have two or more.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Walk"] -->|"no repeated edges"| B["Trail"]
    B -->|"no repeated vertices"| C["Path"]
    A -->|"starts = ends"| D["Closed Walk"]
    D -->|"no repeated edges"| E["Circuit"]
    E -->|"no repeated vertices"| F["Cycle"]
sections.caption: The hierarchy of walks: each restriction from left to right is a special case of the one before it.

sections.title: Trees — The Most Important Special Case
sections.content:
A **tree** is a connected acyclic undirected graph. Trees are perhaps the most pervasive data structure in computer science: binary search trees, parse trees, file-system hierarchies, HTML DOMs, decision trees — all are trees in the graph-theoretic sense.

The central theorem about trees has three equivalent characterisations of a tree on n vertices, any two of which imply the third:
1. T is connected and acyclic.
2. T is connected and has exactly n − 1 edges.
3. T is acyclic and has exactly n − 1 edges.

Why n − 1? Build a tree inductively: start with a single vertex (0 edges). To connect each new vertex, you need exactly one new edge (adding it to any existing vertex keeps the graph connected and acyclic). After n vertices, you have used n − 1 edges. Adding any additional edge between two already-connected vertices creates exactly one cycle (since the tree already has a unique path between them, the new edge completes a loop).

A **forest** is an acyclic graph (not necessarily connected) — a disjoint union of trees. A forest on n vertices and k connected components has exactly n − k edges.

A **rooted tree** designates one vertex as the **root**. This induces a parent-child relationship: on the unique path from the root to any vertex, the preceding vertex is the **parent**. Vertices with no children are **leaves**. The **height** of a tree is the length of the longest path from root to leaf; the **depth** of a vertex is its distance from the root.

A **spanning tree** of a connected graph G is a subgraph that includes all vertices of G and is itself a tree. Every connected graph has at least one spanning tree. Finding a spanning tree of minimum total edge weight is the **minimum spanning tree (MST)** problem, solved by Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms.

sections.title: Graph Representations in Code
sections.content:
Before discussing algorithms we need to choose how to represent a graph in memory. The two standard choices have different trade-offs.

An **adjacency matrix** is a |V| × |V| boolean (or weighted) matrix where `matrix[u][v] = 1` (or the edge weight) if an edge (u, v) exists, and 0 otherwise. **Pros**: O(1) edge lookup (`does edge u→v exist?`); easy to implement. **Cons**: O(V²) space regardless of how many edges exist — catastrophic for sparse graphs where |E| ≪ |V|². Checking all neighbours of a vertex takes O(V) time even if the vertex has degree 2.

An **adjacency list** stores for each vertex a list (or array) of its neighbours. **Pros**: O(V + E) space — proportional to what actually exists; iterating over a vertex's neighbours takes O(degree(v)) time. **Cons**: O(degree(v)) time to check if a specific edge exists (requires scanning the list). For most graph algorithms — BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, topological sort — we iterate over neighbours repeatedly and rarely need O(1) edge lookup, so adjacency lists win in practice.

A **weighted adjacency list** stores `{vertex, weight}` pairs instead of just vertex indices. In JavaScript this is naturally a `Map<vertex, Array<{to, weight}>>`.

For very sparse graphs (like road networks where each intersection touches ~4 roads), adjacency lists use a tiny fraction of the memory that adjacency matrices would require. For dense graphs (|E| ≈ |V|²), the difference is less important and matrices may be simpler to code.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: BFS uses a queue (FIFO) to explore the graph level by level, guaranteeing that the first time a vertex is reached it is via the shortest path (fewest edges). DFS uses the call stack (recursion) to go as deep as possible before backtracking — useful for detecting cycles, computing topological order, and finding connected components. Both run in O(V + E) time with an adjacency list.

sections.title: Eulerian Paths and Circuits — the Seven Bridges Problem
sections.content:
In 1736, the citizens of Königsberg (now Kaliningrad, Russia) wondered whether they could walk through the city crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once. Leonhard Euler proved it was impossible — and in doing so founded graph theory.

Euler modelled the problem as a graph: land masses as vertices, bridges as edges. He asked: does a **trail** exist that traverses every edge exactly once? Such a trail is called an **Eulerian path** if it starts and ends at different vertices, or an **Eulerian circuit** if it starts and ends at the same vertex.

**Euler's Theorem (undirected graphs):**
- A connected graph has an **Eulerian circuit** if and only if every vertex has **even degree**.
- A connected graph has an **Eulerian path** (but not circuit) if and only if it has **exactly two vertices of odd degree** — those two vertices are the endpoints.

The intuition: when the path arrives at a vertex it must also leave (except at the start and end). So every intermediate vertex must have equal numbers of arrival and departure edges — an even degree. Only the start (one extra departure) and end (one extra arrival) can have odd degree.

Königsberg had four land masses with degrees 3, 3, 3, 5 — four odd-degree vertices. Since it had more than two odd-degree vertices, no Eulerian path of any kind was possible.

**Euler's Theorem (directed graphs):**
- A connected digraph has an **Eulerian circuit** iff every vertex has in-degree = out-degree.
- A connected digraph has an **Eulerian path** from u to v iff: out-degree(u) = in-degree(u) + 1, in-degree(v) = out-degree(v) + 1, and all other vertices have in-degree = out-degree.

Finding an actual Eulerian circuit when one exists can be done in O(V + E) using **Hierholzer's algorithm**: repeatedly find sub-circuits and splice them together.

The Eulerian condition is completely determined by vertex degrees — a simple O(V + E) check. This makes Eulerian problems tractable and elegant.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Count odd-degree vertices"] --> B{"How many?"}    
    B -->|"0"| C["Eulerian Circuit exists\nstart anywhere"]
    B -->|"2"| D["Eulerian Path exists\nstart and end at the odd-degree vertices"]
    B -->|"4 or more"| E["No Eulerian Path\nor Circuit possible"]
sections.caption: The degree test for Eulerian existence is O(V + E) and completely determines the answer — no backtracking or full traversal needed.

sections.title: Hamiltonian Paths — The NP-Complete Cousin
sections.content:
A **Hamiltonian path** visits every **vertex** exactly once (unlike Eulerian which visits every **edge**). A **Hamiltonian cycle** is a Hamiltonian path that returns to the starting vertex.

At first glance this looks like a small variation on the Eulerian problem. In reality, it is a completely different beast. While Eulerian existence is determined in linear time by a simple degree check, determining whether a Hamiltonian cycle exists is **NP-complete** — no polynomial-time algorithm is known (and the P ≠ NP conjecture says none exists).

Why the dramatic difference? Eulerian paths are about edge traversal — a local property that each edge independently satisfies. Hamiltonian paths are about vertex ordering — a global property where the choice of which vertex to visit next has cascading effects on the entire path. The problem is essentially equivalent to the **Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP)**: find the shortest route that visits every city exactly once.

There are partial results. **Dirac's theorem** (1952): if every vertex in a simple graph on n ≥ 3 vertices has degree ≥ n/2, then the graph is Hamiltonian. But this is a sufficient condition only — many Hamiltonian graphs do not satisfy it. There is no known characterisation of Hamiltonian graphs that is both necessary and sufficient and efficiently checkable.

For competitive programming and interviews, the key fact is: if you can reduce your problem to Eulerian reachability, you get a polynomial solution; if it requires Hamiltonian paths, you are in NP-complete territory and need heuristics, approximations, or brute force.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The Euler check is a clean O(V) loop — just count odd-degree vertices. The Hamiltonian brute force is O((n-1)!) which makes it completely impractical beyond about n=15. This stark contrast illustrates one of the most important dividing lines in algorithm complexity: the difference between P (Eulerian) and NP-complete (Hamiltonian).

sections.title: Graph Colouring and Bipartite Graphs
sections.content:
A **graph colouring** assigns a colour (from some set of k colours) to each vertex such that no two adjacent vertices share the same colour. The **chromatic number** χ(G) is the minimum number of colours needed.

Colouring models resource allocation problems: register allocation in compilers (two variables that are simultaneously live cannot share a register, so model as a graph and colour it), exam scheduling (two exams with a common student cannot be in the same slot), frequency assignment in wireless networks (adjacent cells need different frequencies), and map colouring (adjacent countries need different colours).

A graph is **2-colourable** — also called **bipartite** — if and only if it contains no odd-length cycle. A bipartite graph has its vertices partitioned into two sets U and V such that every edge goes from U to V (no edges within U or within V). Examples: trees (always bipartite, because trees have no cycles at all), complete bipartite graphs K_{m,n}, the graph of a checkerboard.

BFS 2-colouring is the standard algorithm to check bipartiteness: assign colour 0 to the source, then assign the opposite colour to each neighbour, and check for conflicts. An odd cycle is detected exactly when a vertex is assigned a colour that conflicts with its already-assigned neighbour.

For general graphs: trees and forests need at most 2 colours. Planar graphs need at most 4 colours — the famous **Four Colour Theorem**, proved with computer assistance in 1976 by Appel and Haken. It took mathematicians over a century to prove after Francis Guthrie conjectured it in 1852. Complete graphs K_n need exactly n colours (every vertex is adjacent to every other). **Brooks' theorem** says any connected graph other than an odd cycle or complete graph can be coloured with at most Δ colours, where Δ is the maximum degree.

Finding the chromatic number of a general graph is NP-complete, but 2-colouring (bipartite check) is linear time, and 3-colouring is NP-complete. The jump from 2 to 3 is another example of a dramatic complexity transition.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Bipartite Check via BFS"] --> B["Assign colour 0 to source"]
    B --> C["For each neighbour: assign opposite colour"]
    C --> D{"Conflict found?"}
    D -->|"YES: same colour as neighbour"| E["Not bipartite\nodd cycle exists"]
    D -->|"NO: all vertices coloured"| F["Bipartite graph\nχ(G) = 2"]
sections.caption: BFS 2-colouring: the algorithm checks bipartiteness in O(V + E) time by alternating colours across each edge.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The tree check uses the theorem: a graph is a tree iff it has n-1 edges AND is connected. Two conditions, each O(V+E). The bipartite check handles disconnected graphs by iterating over all vertices as potential BFS roots — if any component has an odd cycle, the whole graph is not bipartite. All trees are bipartite because trees have no cycles at all (let alone odd ones).

sections.title: Topological Sort — Ordering Dependencies in DAGs
sections.content:
A **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** is a directed graph with no directed cycles. DAGs model dependencies: task A must complete before task B, course A is a prerequisite for course B, package A must be installed before package B. The question is: can we find a linear ordering of all vertices such that for every directed edge u → v, u appears before v in the ordering? Such an ordering is called a **topological sort** (or topological order).

Topological sort is only defined for DAGs. If a graph has a directed cycle, no valid topological ordering exists — the nodes in the cycle all depend on each other with no valid starting point.

There are two standard algorithms:

**DFS-based topological sort**: Run DFS on the entire graph. When you finish visiting a vertex (after all its descendants have been visited), push it onto a stack. The stack, read top-to-bottom, gives a valid topological order. This works because a vertex is pushed only after all vertices it points to have been pushed — guaranteeing they appear earlier when the stack is reversed.

**Kahn's algorithm (BFS-based)**: Repeatedly remove vertices with in-degree 0 from the graph (add them to the output, then reduce the in-degree of their neighbours). If a cycle exists, you get stuck — some vertices never reach in-degree 0. If all vertices are eventually output, the output order is a valid topological sort. Both algorithms run in O(V + E).

Topological sort is the backbone of build systems (make, ninja), package managers (npm, pip), course scheduling, and compiler instruction ordering. Any time you have a problem of the form 'do things in the right order given dependencies', think DAG + topological sort.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["In-degree 0 vertices: start here"] --> B["Add to output"]
    B --> C["Reduce in-degree of neighbours"]
    C --> D{"Any new in-degree 0?"}
    D -->|"YES"| A
    D -->|"NO + unprocessed vertices remain"| E["Cycle detected!\nNo topological order"]
    D -->|"NO + all processed"| F["Valid topological order"]
sections.caption: Kahn's algorithm (BFS-based topological sort): process vertices with no remaining prerequisites first, propagating readiness to dependents.

sections.content: **Historical context**: Euler's 1736 paper on the Seven Bridges of Königsberg is considered the first theorem in graph theory. The term 'graph' was introduced by James Joseph Sylvester in 1878. The Four Colour Theorem, conjectured in 1852, was not proved until 1976 — and required checking 1,936 cases with a computer program, the first major theorem proved with computer assistance. Graph theory now touches nearly every subfield of computer science: networking (routing protocols are shortest-path algorithms on weighted graphs), databases (query optimisation uses DAGs), machine learning (neural networks, graphical models), social network analysis (centrality, community detection), and compiler design (control flow graphs, register allocation).

sections.title: Connectivity, Components, and Strongly Connected Components
sections.content:
For undirected graphs, **connectivity** is straightforward: run BFS or DFS from any vertex. If all vertices are reached, the graph is connected; otherwise, each call to BFS/DFS from an unvisited vertex reveals a new **connected component**.

For directed graphs, connectivity is more nuanced. A digraph is **weakly connected** if the underlying undirected graph (ignoring edge directions) is connected. It is **strongly connected** if there is a directed path from every vertex to every other vertex — you can reach everywhere and return from everywhere.

A **strongly connected component (SCC)** of a digraph is a maximal set of vertices such that there is a directed path between every pair. Every vertex belongs to exactly one SCC. The SCCs of a DAG are all single vertices (no cycles means no mutual reachability).

Finding all SCCs can be done in O(V + E) using **Kosaraju's algorithm** (two DFS passes: one on the original graph, one on the reversed graph in reverse finish-time order) or **Tarjan's algorithm** (single DFS pass using a stack and low-link values). The condensation of a graph — replacing each SCC with a single super-vertex — is always a DAG. This is useful because it lets you analyse the high-level structure of any digraph by first decomposing it into SCCs.

SCCs appear in page rank (web pages linking to each other), software module analysis (circular dependencies), and deadlock detection in concurrent systems (threads waiting on each other form a cycle in the wait-for graph).

**Common interview traps and misconceptions to know cold:**

**Eulerian vs Hamiltonian**: Eulerian visits every *edge* once (polynomial, check degrees); Hamiltonian visits every *vertex* once (NP-complete). Confusing the two in an interview is a major red flag.

**Trees**: Any two of the three conditions (connected, acyclic, |E| = |V|-1) imply the third. You don't need to check all three.

**BFS vs DFS**: BFS finds shortest paths by hop count in unweighted graphs. DFS is better for cycle detection, topological sort, and SCC finding. Both are O(V+E) with adjacency lists.

**Bipartite check shortcut**: A graph is bipartite iff it has no odd-length cycles. Equivalently, iff BFS 2-colouring succeeds. Trees are always bipartite.

**Directed vs undirected degree**: For directed graphs, in-degree ≠ out-degree in general. The handshaking lemma for directed graphs: Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E| (not 2|E|).

**Topological sort only on DAGs**: If a directed graph has a cycle, no topological order exists. Kahn's algorithm detects cycles as a bonus: if output size < |V|, a cycle exists.

items: A **graph** G=(V, E) is a set of vertices and edges. Graphs can be undirected or directed, weighted or unweighted. **Adjacency lists** use O(V+E) space and are standard for sparse graphs; adjacency matrices use O(V²) and are better when edges are dense or O(1) edge-existence lookup is needed.
The **handshaking lemma**: Σ deg(v) = 2|E| for undirected graphs; the number of odd-degree vertices is always even. For digraphs: Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E|.

**Trees** are connected acyclic graphs with exactly |V|−1 edges. Any two of {connected, acyclic, |E|=|V|−1} imply the third. All trees are bipartite; a spanning tree of a connected graph always exists.

**Eulerian circuit** exists iff the graph is connected and every vertex has even degree (O(V+E) check). **Eulerian path** exists iff exactly two vertices have odd degree. **Hamiltonian cycle** is NP-complete — no polynomial characterisation exists.
**BFS** finds shortest paths by hop count in O(V+E) in unweighted graphs. **DFS** detects cycles, finds SCCs, and computes topological sort. Both use O(V+E) time with adjacency lists.

A graph is **bipartite** (2-colourable) iff it has no odd-length cycle — detected by BFS 2-colouring in O(V+E). Graph **chromatic number** χ(G) is NP-complete to compute in general, but 2-colouring is linear.
**Topological sort** linearly orders vertices of a DAG respecting all edge directions. Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees) and DFS post-order both work in O(V+E) and detect cycles as a side-effect.

quiz.question: A graph has 5 vertices with degrees 2, 3, 3, 4, 4. How many edges does it have?
quiz.explanation: By the handshaking lemma: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|. Sum of degrees = 2+3+3+4+4 = 16. So |E| = 16/2 = 8. The sum must always be even, confirming that the number of odd-degree vertices (degrees 3 and 3) is even — two odd-degree vertices here.

quiz.question: A connected graph with n vertices that is also acyclic must have how many edges?
options: n
n²/2
quiz.explanation: A connected acyclic graph is a tree. Trees have exactly n−1 edges. You need at least n−1 edges for connectivity (a spanning tree), and adding any further edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle — so acyclicity forces the count to be exactly n−1. This is one of the three equivalent characterisations of trees.

quiz.question: Which condition guarantees an Eulerian circuit exists in a connected undirected graph?
options: Every vertex has degree at least 2
The graph has no cycles
Every vertex has even degree
Exactly two vertices have odd degree
quiz.explanation: Euler's theorem: a connected undirected graph has an Eulerian circuit (traverse every edge exactly once, returning to start) if and only if every vertex has even degree. Exactly two odd-degree vertices gives an Eulerian PATH (not circuit) with those two as endpoints. Four or more odd-degree vertices means no Eulerian path or circuit exists at all.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between an Eulerian circuit and a Hamiltonian cycle?
options: Eulerian visits every vertex once; Hamiltonian visits every edge once
Eulerian visits every edge once; Hamiltonian visits every vertex once
Both visit every vertex and edge once, but differ only in direction
Eulerian requires a weighted graph; Hamiltonian does not
quiz.explanation: An Eulerian circuit traverses every EDGE exactly once (returning to start). A Hamiltonian cycle visits every VERTEX exactly once (returning to start). This subtle difference makes Eulerian problems solvable in polynomial time (check vertex degrees) while Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete with no known efficient characterisation.

quiz.question: BFS from a source vertex in an unweighted graph guarantees which property?
options: It finds shortest paths by total edge weight
It finds shortest paths by number of edges (hop count)
It produces a minimum spanning tree
It always visits vertices in alphabetical order
quiz.explanation: BFS explores the graph level by level using a FIFO queue. The first time a vertex is reached, it is via the fewest possible edges. This gives correct shortest paths by hop count for unweighted graphs. For weighted graphs you need Dijkstra (non-negative weights) or Bellman-Ford (allows negative weights).

quiz.question: A directed graph has |V|=6 and |E|=9. What is the sum of all out-degrees?
quiz.explanation: In a directed graph, each edge contributes exactly 1 to the out-degree of its source vertex. Therefore Σ out-degree = |E| = 9. Similarly, Σ in-degree = |E| = 9. The sum of ALL degrees (in + out) = 2|E| = 18. This is the directed version of the handshaking lemma.

quiz.question: A bipartite graph can always be coloured with at most how many colours, and why?
options: 1 colour — all vertices are equivalent
2 colours — vertices split into two sets, all edges cross between them
3 colours — bipartite graphs may contain triangles
4 colours — the Four Colour Theorem applies
quiz.explanation: A bipartite graph partitions vertices into sets U and V such that all edges go between U and V (none within). Colour every vertex in U with colour 1 and every vertex in V with colour 2 — no two adjacent vertices share a colour. Bipartite graphs contain no odd-length cycles, which is the precise characterisation of 2-colourability. Trees are a special case.

quiz.question: The handshaking lemma implies which surprising fact about any undirected graph?
options: Every graph must have at least one isolated vertex
The number of vertices with odd degree is always even
Every undirected graph is bipartite
The sum of degrees equals the number of vertices
quiz.explanation: Since Σ deg(v) = 2|E| is always even, and the even-degree vertices contribute an even total, the odd-degree vertices must together contribute an even number — which requires an even count of them. This means you can never have exactly 1, 3, 5, or any odd number of odd-degree vertices in any undirected graph.

quiz.question: Topological sort is defined only for which type of graph?
options: Any connected undirected graph
Any graph with at least one cycle
Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) only
Complete graphs only
quiz.explanation: Topological sort produces a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge u→v, u appears before v. This is only possible when the graph has no directed cycles — if a cycle exists (A→B→C→A), then A must precede B, B must precede C, and C must precede A — a contradiction. Kahn's algorithm detects this: if output size < |V|, a cycle exists.

quiz.question: Which algorithm correctly detects whether an undirected graph is bipartite in linear time?
options: DFS with post-order numbering to find back edges
BFS 2-colouring: assign alternating colours and check for conflicts
Dijkstra's shortest path from the highest-degree vertex
Kahn's topological sort on the undirected version
quiz.explanation: BFS 2-colouring assigns colour 0 to the source, then alternates colours across each edge. If a vertex is about to be assigned a colour that conflicts with its already-coloured neighbour (same colour), an odd cycle has been found and the graph is not bipartite. The algorithm runs in O(V+E) and handles disconnected graphs by iterating over all unvisited vertices as new BFS roots.
